desc:
In one operation you may swap two neighbouring elements of nums. Using at most k operations, make the array lexicographically as large as possible (compare element by element from the left) and return it.

nums = [3, 9, 1, 2], k = 2
result = [9, 3, 2, 1]

nums = [1, 2, 3], k = 1
result = [2, 1, 3]
hints: The first position matters most. Which values can reach position 0 with at most k adjacent swaps?

Only the elements in the window nums[0..k] can reach position 0, at a cost equal to their index. Pick the largest value in that window; if it occurs more than once, pick the leftmost copy because it is cheaper.
Move the chosen element to the front, subtract its distance from k, and repeat for position 1 with the new budget, then position 2, and so on until the budget is used up.
editorial: Greedy by position. For the current position i and remaining budget k, the candidates that can still be brought to i are the elements at indices i .. min(n - 1, i + k). Taking the largest candidate gives the best possible value for this position, and no later position can compensate for a smaller one.

Ties are broken toward the leftmost copy: the value is the same but the move is cheaper, leaving more budget for later positions. Moving an element from index j to i by adjacent swaps shifts the elements i .. j-1 one cell to the right and costs exactly j - i. This is a pop and an insert on the list.

Each position scans a window of up to min(n, k + 1) elements and shifts up to n elements, so the time is O(n2) (a few milliseconds for n = 3,000 with built-in slicing, or O(n log n) with a segment tree plus a Fenwick tree for the shifts). Because the window is clipped at the end of the array, k = 109 is handled without any special case.
